catalog_locator: pp. 155-156, §7.3.4 'Tone systems' and §7.3.5 'Rhythm and intonation' (the scan's heading reads '7.3.55'); the 155/156 page break is inferred from the running head '156 Naden' that falls inside the first sentence of §7.3.5 (chapter span 141-168). Text recovered from Open Library search-inside excerpts of archive.org item nigercongolangua0000unse (lending-only; no seen).
catalog_quote: [§7.3.4, p.155] It may well be that an alternative analysis on entirely different principles, as yet undiscovered, is needed to account for Gur pitch and accentual phenomena. [§7.3.5, pp.155-156] Stress-accent is not a feature of Gur languages; the characteristic rhythm is syllable-timed with high tone, intonation peak, and vowel length determining the prominence of syllabics. Even among closely related languages there may be clear differences, for instance the alternation of long and short vowels gives a kind of rocking rhythm to MR and MP in contrast to the more staccato effect of DB, where most vowels are short; the glottal breaking of long vowels is the salient feature of FR. [chapter language checklist] MP* Mampruli (Mampelle, mampulli) - C, Gh

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: contains the quoted 7.3.5 passage verbatim at the stated locator (pp.155-156, running head '156 Naden' inside sentence 1). Because that file is a reconstruction, I re-derived it from the raw evidence: parsing showed every clause of the quote covered by archive.org scanned highlights from item nigercongolangua0000unse EXCEPT one ('the characteristic rhythm is syllable-timed with high tone, intonation peak, and vowel length'), which the compilers had inserted without a saved snippet. I re-queried openlibrary.org/search/ myself (responses saved as in the same folder) and that clause is now attested verbatim by v1-v4 ('..of Gur languages; the characteristic rhythm is syllable-timed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: According to Naden (the principal Mampruli fieldworker), Gur languages including Mampruli (MP) have no stress-accent; rhythm is syllable-timed and syllable prominence is a by-product of high tone, intonation peaks and vowel length; Mampruli's long/short vowel alternation gives it a 'rocking' rhythm (vs. 'staccato' Dagbani). Tone exists (two tones H/L per the WALDS sheet as coded in PHOIBLE; Naden 1986:260 says tone 'plays a very limited functional role' in these languages and is not written).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the passage is a family-level generalisation with a Mampruli-specific remark on rhythm only.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-survey statement (Gur as a whole) in which Mampruli is named only for its vowel-length rhythm; no word-level stress rule is given anywhere in the accessible Mampruli-specific descriptions (grammar sketch, spelling guide, dictionary, 1980 phonology article), which are silent on stress. Text was recovered from archive.org full-text-search highlights of a lending-only scan, not from viewed page scan.
new_statements.identity_note: All Naden materials describe the western-central dialect (Walewale-Gbeduuri area) of Mampruli [mamp1244]; the Naden 1989 statement is a Gur-family generalisation that names Mampruli (MP) only for its vowel-length rhythm.
